To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
hypocalcemia decreases EGFR density and autophos-phorylation, which can be normalized by calcium supplementation, and that this normalization is independent of the vitamin D hormone.
hypocalcemia decreases EGFR density and its autophosphorytion in normal liver, and that this effect is independent of vitamin D3.

hypocalcemia in the absence of vitamin D (1,25-( OH)2D3) deficiency decreases epidermal-growth-factor receptor (EGFR), density and autophophorylation in rat liver, but the latter is restored when calcium alone is supplemented to the hypocalcemic diet.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the calcium and/or D3-dependent mechanisms associated with liver regeneration.
the initial signaling events of the EGF receptor in normal rat liver.
the identification of the calcium- and D3-dependent events involved in the regulation of the initial steps of the EGF signaling cascade in normal rat liver.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

hypocalcemia is the primary signal responsible for the decreased EGFR number and subsequent autophosphyolation, whereas the D3 hormone is the secondary signal that restores the EGFR number and autophosphyilation in the liver.

the hypocalcemic state, regardless of the prevailing D3 status, decreases hepatic EGF responsiveness by reducing EGFR density and its subsequent phosphorylation, which is fully reversible by calcium supplementation.
the D hormone and calcium, either separately or in combination, have a profound influence on the initial events transducing the EGF signal in liver.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the calcium status, rather than the D3 status per se, is the major determinant of EGFR density and autophophorylation.

hypocalcemia and/or D deficiency perturbs EGFR density, which in turn leads to decreased EGFR autophorylation, which in itself may be responsible for the observed decrease in the proliferative response.
hypocalcemia and D deficiency, acting through a common pathway, perturb the initial transduction steps of EGF, which is a potent stimulator of hepatic growth.
The main takeaway from our work is that
hypocalcemia and D deficiency are two independent and distinct factors affecting the EGFR number and autophosphyration.
hypocalcemia is the major determinant of the observed changes in hepatic EGFR density and autophorylation.
hypocalcemia is a key regulator of EGFR in normal rat liver, and that normalization of calcium is required to achieve full restoration of EGF signaling in D-deficient rats.
